agree.reason: The letter is candid and readable, but it reads like every other teacher's letter: it never shows the signed training records, the two clean state audits or the GMP course, so a skeptical HR manager has little reason to move it into the phone-screen pile.

honest.reason: It rightly drops the unprovable 'cut training time in half' claim and keeps the real numbers accurate, but it adds small details the brief doesn't support, such as checks on whether the procedures are being followed, 'teenagers using hazardous materials for the first time', and 'showing with records' (which it never backs up).

works_the_facts.reason: The figures are only restated: it doesn't present 41% to 58% as a 17-point (about 40% relative) gain, and it misses the strongest fact, the cut of new-teacher training from 20 hours to 12 (a 40% reduction), which is exactly the result this employer cares about.

right_comparison.reason: It never shows a before-and-after, such as the 20-hour training it replaced, and never compares itself with a conventional GMP-experienced hire, so the reader has no baseline to judge improvement against.

qualification.reason: The only hedge is a vague promise to learn their system before changing anything; it leaves out the checkable details the reader needs: the GMP course finishing May 2, the June 14 start date and interview availability.

objections.reason: It raises the expected 'no regulated-industry or GMP experience' objection itself but answers it weakly, leaving out the signed training records, two clean state audits and GMP enrollment that would actually answer it.

fit.reason: It is a one-page cover letter in the right form, but it uses 'Dear Hiring Manager' instead of Karen Doyle, never names Calder Pharmaceuticals, and has no signature name.
